raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Problem

Since the frontend started keeping runtime-compiled plans alive for the CUDA graphs that record them, a destroyed CUDA graph hands its plan back through a CUDA user-object destructor. That destructor may not call CUDA, so the plan is queued, and the queue was drained by the next `execute()` on a stream that is not being captured.

Releasing a plan destroys its backend descriptor, which frees device memory and unloads its runtime-compiled code. Both wait for all work on the device. So an otherwise asynchronous `execute()`, of any plan, could:

- block until unrelated work on other streams finished, or
- deadlock, if that work waited for the application to continue after the call (for example a host callback waiting on a flag).

Measured on H100: unloading code or freeing memory while another stream has 600 ms of pending work takes 580–910 ms, against 0.02 ms when the device is idle. Doing it from another thread doesn't help, because launches from other threads stall for the same time.

## Fix

Drain the queue when a `CudaGraphRetainedResource` is destroyed, that is when the frontend destroys an execution plan or graph, right after the owner drops its own reference. `execute()` and capture only add references to the graph being recorded.

- A CUDA graph still keeps its plan (and host-copy data such as ALiBi slopes) alive for as long as the graph exists. Only the release of plans whose graphs are already gone moves.
- A plan whose graphs outlive every frontend plan and graph stays alive until the next one is destroyed, or until process exit.
- A matching change to the cuDNN backend, for the code it releases itself, is in progress. That change alone isn't enough for frontend users, because the frontend would still destroy the plan inside `execute()`.

## Tests

The CUDA graph lifetime tests move from `samples/cpp/misc/cudagraphs.cpp`, which is meant as a sample, to the unit tests in a new `test/cpp/cuda_graph_lifetime.cpp` (second commit, moved unchanged). The sample file keeps "Cuda graphs with matmul add". New tests there:

- **Retained resources are released when an owner is destroyed:** with a payload that counts its releases, a graph that outlives its owner keeps the payload; recording on an uncaptured stream (what `execute()` does) releases nothing; destroying any owner releases it. An owner that outlives its graphs releases the payload in its own destructor.
- **Executing a frontend graph does not release what CUDA graphs handed back:** three uncaptured `execute()` calls leave a queued release pending; destroying the frontend graph releases it.

Run on H100 against a cuDNN 9.29 dev build: the 6 `[cudagraph]` cases in `tests` and the 3 in `samples` pass, and so does the rest of `tests` (62 cases: 60 passed, 2 skipped). The `[cudagraph]` cases include "Cuda graph outlives the frontend graph" and "ALiBi slopes outlive the frontend graph in a CUDA graph", which check that graphs keep their plans alive. With the old headers, the new tests fail at the three expected points.

files.patch:
@@ -62,6 +62,6 @@ For an example usage of these functions in C++, refer to the [cudagraphs.cpp](ht
 
 A CUDA graph recorded from a frontend graph, whether through `populate_cuda_graph()`/`update_cuda_graph()` or through CUDA stream capture around `execute()`, keeps launching that graph's execution plan for as long as the CUDA graph, any clone of it, or any `cudaGraphExec_t` instantiated from it exists. For execution plans whose engine compiles its kernels at runtime (behavior note `RUNTIME_COMPILATION`), the frontend therefore gives the CUDA graph a reference to the execution plan (a CUDA user object), so the plan and the kernel code it owns stay alive until the last such CUDA graph is destroyed, even if the application destroys the frontend graph first. Plans of precompiled engines need no such reference, since their kernels are part of the cuDNN library, and are recorded without one. No action is needed from the application; in particular it is safe to drop the frontend graph right after recording. Note that cuDNN releases runtime-compiled kernel code together with the execution plan, so without this reference a replay after the frontend graph was destroyed could run stale code. The same holds for host data that the recorded graph copies to the device on every replay, such as the ALiBi slopes that the frontend computes on the host: the CUDA graph holds a reference to it as well.
 
-The plan is released on the next `execute()` that is not being captured (releasing it during a capture would invalidate the capture). An application that records a graph and never executes through the frontend again keeps that plan alive until process exit.
+Once the last such CUDA graph is gone, the plan is released the next time the frontend destroys an execution plan or graph of its own. Releasing a plan waits for all work on the device, so it is kept out of `execute()`, which would otherwise block on unrelated streams. An application that records a graph and never destroys another frontend graph keeps that plan alive until process exit.
 
 The reference is a CUDA user object attached to the CUDA graph. CUDA graphs that carry user objects take a slightly slower launch path; on tiny graphs this has been measured at roughly 1-2 microseconds of additional replay latency per launch (H100, CUDA 13), which is negligible for graphs of realistic size but visible in micro-benchmarks that replay a single small kernel.
